objectives.text: Explain the operating system's goals, boundaries, and place among computer-system components.
Trace instruction and I/O data flow through CPU registers, memory, controllers, and device drivers.
Analyze how interrupts transfer control and improve processor utilization during I/O.
Compare sequential and priority-based handling of multiple interrupts and relate OS user and system views.
Compare storage levels and select programmed, interrupt-driven, or DMA I/O from transfer requirements.
Differentiate single-processor, multiprocessor, multicore, NUMA, and clustered architectures.
Explain bootstrap, interrupt-driven OS operation, multiprogramming, and time sharing.
Apply dual-mode and timer mechanisms to operating-system protection scenarios.
Distinguish programs, processes, threads, concurrency, and process-management responsibilities.
Explain OS memory, file, mass-storage, cache, protection, and security management.
Compare virtualization, distributed-system models, and networked computing environments.
Differentiate real-time constraints and interrupt classes and reason about privileged operations.
Classify OS services for users, programs, and efficient shared-system operation.
Compare CLI, GUI, and touch interfaces and their command-execution models.
Trace API calls through the run-time and system-call interface, including parameter passing.
Classify system calls and trace a robust file-copy sequence with error handling.
Differentiate system services, background services, and application programs.
Trace compilation, linking, loading, OS-specific execution, and contrasting Arduino and FreeBSD behavior.
Relate OS goals, policy/mechanism separation, and implementation-language trade-offs.
Compare monolithic, layered, microkernel, modular, and hybrid OS structures.
Trace OS build and boot processes and distinguish logs, core dumps, crash dumps, tracing, and performance tuning.
Explain process memory layout, execution state, and lifecycle transitions.
Identify PCB fields and relate them to Linux task_struct and context preservation.
Analyze threads, multithreading benefits, process scheduling, and queue migration.
Explain context switches and the isolation benefits of multiprocess browser architecture.
Trace UNIX process creation, execution choices, and termination states.
Compare IPC models and apply the bounded-buffer shared-memory protocol.
Explain message-passing links, send/receive operations, and implementation choices.
Compare direct and indirect naming, synchronization, and buffering semantics.
Apply pipe and socket properties to process and network communication scenarios.
Explain CPU-I/O burst behavior, scheduler decisions, and preemption.
Apply dispatcher and scheduling criteria to performance goals.
Trace FCFS schedules, waiting times, turnaround times, and convoy effects.
Apply nonpreemptive SJF and explain burst prediction by exponential averaging.
Compare preemptive SRTF with nonpreemptive SJF through arrival-time traces.
Apply round-robin timing, bounds, and numerical schedules.
Analyze round-robin quantum effects on switches and turnaround.
Apply priority scheduling, aging, and priority-plus-RR rules.
Compare multilevel queue and feedback-queue movement policies.
Compare asymmetric and symmetric multiprocessor scheduling structures.
Analyze multicore hardware threads, load balancing, affinity, and NUMA placement.
Evaluate scheduling algorithms with deterministic, queueing, simulation, and implementation methods.
Explain races, critical sections, and the three critical-section requirements.
Trace Peterson’s two-process protocol and justify its mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting properties.
Analyze why instruction reordering can invalidate a software synchronization protocol on modern architectures.
Explain memory barriers, test-and-set, compare-and-swap, and atomic variables.
Apply mutex and semaphore operations to mutual exclusion and event ordering.
Analyze semaphore failure modes and bounded-buffer sequencing.
Interpret resource-allocation graphs and the conditions under which a cycle indicates deadlock.
Compare prevention, avoidance, detection-recovery, and ignoring deadlocks.
Apply prevention protocols that invalidate hold-and-wait, no-preemption, or circular-wait conditions.
Explain safe and unsafe states and resource-allocation graph avoidance.
Use Banker’s data structures, safety algorithm, and resource-request algorithm.
Analyze the supplied Banker’s snapshot and resource requests.
Use wait-for graphs and detection data structures for single and multiple resource instances.
Trace the supplied deadlock-detection example and decide when detection is invoked.
Compare termination and resource-preemption recovery choices and their costs.
Explain memory protection, address binding, logical addresses, physical addresses, and MMU relocation.
Apply contiguous allocation, variable partitions, and dynamic hole-selection rules.
Analyze fragmentation, compaction, and segmentation concepts.
Apply paging address translation, page-table structures, protection, and sharing.
Explain swapping and swapping with paging.
Analyze virtual memory, demand paging, valid-invalid bits, and page-fault handling.

project.title: Operating Systems Study
